passages.title: The scorner who hoards and counts wealth
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat draw a single portrait: a man whose tongue tears down other people, whose hands never stop piling up money, and who imagines that the money has made him permanent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the sūrah as a warning of severe punishment for three grave sins — **backbiting, deriding, and the selfish hoarding of wealth** — followed by a description of the nature of that punishment.

What holds ayat 1–3 together is that they describe one person, not three. Ayah 1 pronounces the woe. Ayah 2 continues with a relative clause — *alladhī*, "**the one who** amasses wealth and counts it" — describing the same person already condemned in ayah 1. Ayah 3 then tells us what that person thinks.

---

## Ayah 1: "Woe to every *humazah, lumazah*"

**"Every."** Note that the ayah does not name a person. It says *likulli* — "to **every** *humazah, lumazah*." The door is left open for anyone who fits the description, in any century.

**The two words.** *Humazah* and *lumazah* come from the roots *hamz* and *lamz*, and the commentators do not all draw the line between them in the same place. It is worth hearing the views side by side rather than flattening them:

- **Ibn Kathir** transmits that *al-hammāz* refers to slander **by speech**, and *al-lammāz* to slander **by action**. He notes the Qur'an uses the related word elsewhere — *"Hammāz, going about with slander"* (68:11) — and that the meaning of both is that **the person finds fault with people and belittles them**.
- **Ibn ʿAbbas** said: *"Humazah Lumazah* means one who reviles and disgraces (others)."
- **Mujahid** said: *"Al-Humazah* is with the **hand and the eye**, and *al-Lumazah* is with the **tongue**." (Notice this reverses Ibn Kathir's assignment — for Mujahid it is *humazah* that is gestural and *lumazah* that is verbal.)
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reports that **most commentators** agree that *hamz* means **to backbite** — to speak ill of a person behind his back — and gives *lamz* the sense of **slandering or deriding**, that is, speaking ill of a person **to his face**.

Put together, the ayah closes every escape route. If you thought the sin was only what you say out loud, Mujahid's *"with the hand and the eye"* covers the raised eyebrow, the smirk, the mimicking gesture — the vocabulary of contempt that never becomes a sentence. If you thought it was only what you say to someone's face, *hamz* covers what is said behind their back. And Ibn ʿAbbas's *"reviles and disgraces"* is not limited to lying. What unites all of it is Ibn Kathir's phrase: **finding fault with people and belittling them.**

## Which is worse — behind the back or to the face?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes this up carefully, and refuses to give a one-line answer, because each is worse than the other from a different angle:

**Backbiting is worse from one perspective** because the ill is spoken behind the victim's back. He is not present to defend himself and put an end to it — so the sin continues to be committed, to a greater and increasing degree. From this angle, face-to-face fault-finding is relatively less in degree, precisely because the victim is present and can put a stop to it.

**Deriding to the face is worse from another perspective** because speaking ill of a person to his face amounts to **insulting and denigrating him**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges this to be morally and socially more harmful and hurting, and therefore its punishment more dreadful.

Both, it concludes, are **morally and socially obnoxious and deadly**, and both the Qur'an and the Sunnah have sounded a stern warning against them.

**From the Sunnah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the Prophet ﷺ said that **the worst servants of Allah are those who speak ill of someone, creating enmity between friends and finding fault with innocent people.** Sit with that sentence. The measure named here is not embarrassment caused; it is *friendships broken* and *innocent people made to look guilty*.

---

## Ayat 2–3: the money, and the thought underneath it

**"Who amasses wealth and counts it."** Ibn Kathir explains *jamaʿa mālan wa ʿaddadah* concretely: **he gathers it, piling some of it on top of the rest, and he counts it up.** The image is physical — heaping and tallying. He links it to Allah's words elsewhere, *"And collect (wealth) and hide it"* (70:18), a connection Ibn Kathir attributes to **As-Suddi** and **Ibn Jarir**. Gathering and keeping, then, rather than gathering and spending.

The most piercing comment on this ayah comes from **Muhammad bin Kaʿb**, quoted by Ibn Kathir:

> "His wealth occupies his time in the day, going from this to that. Then when the night comes he sleeps like a rotting corpse."

That is a whole life in one sentence. The day is spent moving from one holding to the next, and the night, in his description, gives back nothing.

**"Thinking that his wealth will make him immortal."** Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayah 3 is precise and easy to skate past: he thinks that gathering wealth **will make him last forever in this abode** — that is, in the worldly life. Read carefully, this is not a doctrine anyone need say out loud. The ayah does not report a claim he makes; it reports what he *thinks* — what he assumes as he plans, hoards and counts.

---

## An essential qualification: this is not a condemnation of wealth

This is where readers most often go wrong, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses it head-on. **The amassing of wealth is not, in principle, prohibited or sinful** — other verses and aḥādīth bear testimony to that, and ayah 2 must be interpreted in their light. The ayah refers to a particular **love of, and passion for**, wealth that is accumulated and counted over and over again.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies what brings a person under this condemnation. Anyone who:

1. **accumulates wealth and does not pay his obligatory dues**; or
2. has a **greed for wealth that leads him to pride and arrogance**; or
3. has a **love of wealth that engrosses him in hoarding so profoundly that he forgets his religious obligations** —

has his practice **condemned in the strongest terms**, and a person attaching such profound love, greed and passion to material riches will suffer the ruin described in the ayat that follow.

Notice that none of the three is a statement about the size of a person's holdings. Each is a statement about what the wealth has done to him.

---

## Living it

**Audit the tongue, including its silent forms.** Because of Mujahid's reading — *"with the hand and the eye"* — a believer cannot claim safety merely by saying nothing. The imitation, the glance across the room, the gesture that gets the laugh: Ibn Kathir's summary covers it all — **finding fault with people and belittling them**. And the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ conveyed by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives you two diagnostic questions: *Has my speech created enmity between friends? Have I made an innocent person look guilty?*

**Do not settle for the "lesser" sin.** Since Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows that backbiting and face-to-face derision are each worse from a different angle, neither can be treated as the safe alternative to the other.

**Apply Maʿārif's three tests to your wealth, not to its size.** Are the obligatory dues paid? Has the money led to pride and arrogance? Has hoarding it crowded out your religious obligations? These are questions about the heart's posture, and a person of modest means can fail all three while a wealthy person passes them.

**Watch the counting.** Ibn Kathir's gloss singles out not only the gathering but the counting up — the returning to the tally. Muhammad bin Kaʿb's description of a day spent "going from this to that" and a night spent asleep "like a rotting corpse" is worth holding one's own day against.

**Finally, remember what ayah 3 diagnoses.** By Ibn Kathir's reading, the delusion is not that money buys the Hereafter; it is that money makes a person **last forever in this abode** — this worldly life. That thought rarely announces itself. It shows up as an assumption: that with enough put away, nothing is coming that cannot be handled. The ayah names that assumption for what it is — a thought a man *thinks*, and one the sūrah has just placed under woe.

passages.title: Cast into the Crusher: the fire of hearts
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat describe a single place, **Al-Ḥuṭamah**, from the outside inward. First that the man is flung into it (ayah 4), then that no imagination can reach it (ayah 5), then whose Fire it is (ayah 6), then how deep it burns (ayah 7), and finally that there is no way out of it (ayat 8–9).

## Ayah 4: the single word that ends the argument

The passage begins with *kallā*. Ibn Kathir explains it plainly: "the matter is not as he claims, nor as he reckons." It is a rebuttal, not a transition — a flat denial of what the man had been claiming and reckoning, struck down before the sentence even continues.

Ibn Kathir is careful to keep the thread tied to the same person: "the person who gathered wealth and counted it, will be thrown into Al-Ḥuṭamah." It is *his* ending, not a general warning that drifts away from him.

Notice also how he arrives there. The translations render it "tossed" and "thrown." He does not walk in.

## The name that crushes

**Al-Ḥuṭamah** is, as Ibn Kathir says, "one of the descriptive names of the Hellfire. This is because it crushes whoever is in it."

That is worth sitting with. The Qur'an could have simply said "the Fire." The name it chooses here is built from crushing, and Ibn Kathir tells us why: because that is what it does to whoever is inside it.

## Ayah 5: a question that admits defeat

*"And what will make you realize what the Crusher is?"*

The question is addressed to the hearer, and its effect is to stop him. It concedes, before describing anything, that nobody arrives at this by imagining harder. So the definition is not left to us. It is given, in the two ayat that follow.

## Ayah 6: "Allah's kindled Fire"

The answer comes as a naming: *nāru-llāhi l-mūqadah* — rendered "Allah's kindled Fire," and by Ibn Kathir as "The fire of Allah, Al-Muqadah."

Two things are said, and the commentators leave them to stand without elaboration. It is **kindled** — set alight, not smouldering, not neglected. And it is **Allah's**. It is not an impersonal force of nature that happens to await the wrongdoer; it belongs to the One the man never reckoned with.

## Ayah 7: the fire that reaches the heart

This is the heart of the passage, and it is where the commentators slow down.

*allatī taṭṭaliʿu ʿalā l-afʾidah* — the word *afʾidah* means the hearts. Ibn Kathir's rendering is that it "leaps up over the hearts"; another translation gives "rages over the hearts"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "that will peep into the hearts." All three carry the same terrible sense: this Fire does not stop at the surface.

Ibn Kathir preserves two early statements here.

**Thābit al-Bunānī** said: *"It will burn them all the way to their hearts while they are still alive."* Then he said: *"Indeed the torment will reach them."* Then — Ibn Kathir records this — **he cried**. That detail is not decoration. It tells you how these ayat were received: not as information to be catalogued, but as something that broke a man mid-sentence.

**Muhammad bin Kaʿb** said: *"It (the Fire) will devour every part of his body until it reaches his heart and comes to the level of his throat, then it will return to his body."* The horror there is the word *return*. It is a cycle, not an event. There is no point at which the burning has finished its work.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out exactly why the Qur'an highlights the heart. The basic property of fire is to burn every particle of whatever falls into it. When people are put into the Hellfire it will devour every limb and organ of the body until it reaches the heart — *but the person will not die*. This characteristic is especially highlighted, Maʿārif explains, because the fire of this world kills the person even before reaching the heart. What we call the cruelty of fire is in fact bounded: death arrives and ends it. That boundary is absent here. The Fire of the Hereafter reaches the heart while the person is still living, and he experiences the torture of the burning of his own heart while alive.

## Ayat 8–9: sealed, and pillared

Two ayat close the surah and close the door.

**Ayah 8** — *innahā ʿalayhim muʾṣadah*. Ibn Kathir glosses *muʾṣadah* as **covering**, and refers the reader to the same word in Sūrat al-Balad (90:20). It is shut over them.

**Ayah 9** — *fī ʿamadin mumaddadah*, "in pillars stretched forth." Here the early authorities differ on the detail, and Ibn Kathir reports the difference rather than settling it:

- **ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī** said: "Pillars of Iron."
- **As-Suddī** said: "Made of fire."
- **Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās**: "He will make them enter pillars stretched forth, meaning there will be columns over them, and they will have chains on their necks, and the gates (of Hell) will be shut upon them."

Iron or fire, the pillars stand over them either way. Ibn ʿAbbās adds two further images: chains at the neck, and gates shut fast. The man who was thrown in is not going anywhere.

## Living it

Read carelessly, this surah could be heard as a condemnation of having money. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān blocks that reading directly: other verses and Ahadith bear witness that **amassing wealth is in principle not prohibited or sinful**, and the surah must be understood in their light.

So who is it that ends in Al-Ḥuṭamah? Maʿārif names three things, and says that a person who attaches such profound love, greed and passion to material riches "will suffer eternal perdition as described in the verses that follow" — that is, in the very ayat we have just read:

1. **Accumulating wealth and not paying the obligatory dues on it.**
2. **Greed for wealth that leads to pride and arrogance.**
3. **Love of wealth so engrossing that religious obligations are forgotten** — not theft, not fraud, just absorption.

That third one is the quiet one. It requires no crime at all; it only requires being busy.

The practical check this passage puts to a believer is therefore not *how much do I have*, but: do the dues get paid, does the wealth make me proud, and are my obligations to Allah still being kept?

And there is one more thing to take from it, taught not by a ruling but by a man's tears. Thābit al-Bunānī heard these words, said what they meant, and wept. These ayat were never meant to be merely understood.

*Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on Sūrat al-Humazah with all praise and thanks due to Allah, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends with al-ḥamdu lillāh.*
